target_audience: Undergraduate students in Mathematics or Education majors

sections.title: Introduction: The 'Bridge' Metaphor (0:00-0:45)
sections.content: Define mathematical explanation not just as a set of steps, but as a bridge between abstract symbols and intuitive understanding. Introduce the three core criteria: Accuracy, Clarity (Logical Flow), and Accessibility (The Zone of Proximal Development).
sections.example: Visualize a bridge connecting an island of 'Complex Formula' to a land of 'Everyday Reality' using a graphical blueprint.

sections.title: Criterion 1: Precision and Logical Mapping (0:45-2:00)
sections.content: Explain that effective explanations must maintain formal rigor while mapping every symbol to a conceptual entity. Prerequisite check: Students must understand variables as 'placeholders' before viewing them as 'dynamic entities'.
sections.example: Animation showing the Pythagorean theorem: Instead of just c²=a²+b², display a square growing out of each side of a triangle to represent the area visually.

sections.title: Criterion 2: The Power of Multiple Representations (2:00-3:30)
sections.content: Explain the necessity of the 'Rule of Three': Representing a concept algebraically, geometrically, and contextually. This ensures the learner doesn't just memorize, but visualizes.
sections.example: Representing a function: 1. Equation (f(x)=2x), 2. Graphical (a line on a coordinate plane), 3. Contextual (a robot moving at twice the speed of a sloth).

sections.title: Criterion 3: Reducing Cognitive Load via Scaffolding (3:30-4:30)
sections.content: Discuss how to break down complex proofs into digestible 'chunks'. Emphasize the importance of pausing for reflection and using clear, transitional signaling language.
sections.example: An animation of a squirrel 'chunking' nuts into small piles to store, mirroring how an instructor breaks down a multi-step proof into manageable logical 'nuts'.

sections.title: Conclusion: The Feedback Loop (4:30-5:00)
sections.content: Summarize the final criterion: Explanations are iterative. An effective teacher observes the audience's response and adjusts the complexity level dynamically.
sections.example: A flow chart visual showing: Present Concept -> Observe Student Confusion -> Simplify Visual Representation -> Confirm Understanding.
